caseName: Douglas v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., No. 24-CV-1099 (D.C. Ct. App.)
court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
conduct: Appellee Deutsche Bank's brief cited four authorities that did not exist. Attorney Loishirl W. Hall told the court she used Google's generative AI search tool to locate case authority and did not verify the citations; the court struck the brief, referred the matter to disciplinary counsel, and asked its Rules Committee to review sanction authority.

regulatoryOutcome.body: District of Columbia Office of Disciplinary Counsel
regulatoryOutcome.disposition: The Court of Appeals struck appellee's brief and referred the matter to the Office of Disciplinary Counsel for any investigation it deems appropriate. No disciplinary disposition is yet on record.

sources.label: Douglas v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., No. 24-CV-1099 (D.C. Ct. App. 3 Sep 2026), published order PDF via CourtListener storage

summary: In the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, Deutsche Bank's appellee brief cited four nonexistent authorities after counsel used Google's generative AI search tool without verification. The court struck the brief, referred the matter to the Office of Disciplinary Counsel and sent the sanctions-authority question to its Rules Committee.
fabricated: Abadie v. District of Columbia — full fake citation omitted by the court
Cason v. Nat’l Consumer Co-op Bank — full fake citation omitted by the court
Osborne v. District of Columbia — full fake citation omitted by the court
Woods v. United States — full fake citation omitted by the court

courtSaid.quote: Ms. Hall confirmed that four of the brief’s cited authorities did not exist.
She acknowledged that these citations were “not legitimate legal authority” and “should not have appeared in a brief filed with this Court.”

Ms. Hall explained that she had “used Google’s generative artificial intelligence search tool to assist in locating case authority” and did not verify the existence or accuracy of those citations before filing the brief.
As such, we deem it appropriate to strike appellee’s brief. We also refer this matter to the Office of Disciplinary Counsel for any investigation it deems appropriate.

timeline.event: Appeal was submitted for decision without argument.
Court ordered Deutsche Bank to show cause over possibly hallucinated citations.
Hall confirmed four cited authorities did not exist.
Court struck the brief and referred the matter to disciplinary counsel.

whyItMatters: Douglas updates the Mata pattern for appellate practice and search-integrated AI. The tool was not a chatbot named in a prompt; counsel said it was Google's generative AI search tool. The Court of Appeals struck the appellee brief, referred the matter to discipline, and sent the sanctions-authority question to its Rules Committee. The order also put responsibility on every lawyer who signed the brief, not only the lawyer who ran the search, making firm review a live issue.
practiceNote: A law firm brief should have a citation-check step tied to the signer, not to the person who found the case. Search-generated authority should be treated as a lead only. Before filing, each cited case must be opened, read for the proposition, and checked for jurisdiction and status; a firm AI policy should require proof of that review.

caseName: Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya v. Union of India, 2026 INSC 947
court: Supreme Court of India
conduct: An Order-in-Original of the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat, dated 8 October 2025 and imposing a penalty of INR 425.28 crore, relied on judgments and articles that were nonexistent, carried fake citations, or did not support the propositions cited. The Gujarat High Court had dismissed the challenge.

sources.label: Supreme Court of India — Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya v. Union of India, 2026 INSC 947 (official PDF)
Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya v. Union of India, 2026 INSC 947 (Charlotin database archive PDF)

summary: Extending Pooja Ramesh Singh from tribunals to executive adjudicators, the Supreme Court of India set aside a customs penalty order of INR 4.25 billion, and the High Court judgment upholding it, because the order relied on AI-hallucinated precedents. Justice Datta held even an iota of fake material vitiates a decision and left disciplinary action to the officer's appointing authority.
fabricated: several judgments and articles cited in the Order-in-Original dated 8th October, 2025 that were generated using Artificial Intelligence — the Supreme Court did not list them
case laws relied upon by the customs adjudicator that were non-existent or had fake citations — the Supreme Court did not list them
some real case laws relied upon by the customs adjudicator that did not lay down the ratio deduced therefrom — the Supreme Court did not list them

courtSaid.quote: Upon verifying such judgments and articles, it does appear that the second respondent has relied upon case laws that are either non-existent or have fake citations.

A further investigation has also revealed that some of the case laws relied upon by the second respondent, which do exist, do not lay down the ratio deduced therefrom and it appears to be a hallucination of AI.
assistance can never be substituted for adjudication. AI may well serve as training wheels but entrusting it with the pilot’s seat would be both imprudent and dangerous.
the impugned order of the High Court confirming the penalty is consequently set aside together with the Order-in-Original

timeline.event: Additional Commissioner of Customs imposed a Rs. 425,27,99,100 penalty.
Gujarat High Court dismissed Gadiya's challenge to the penalty.
Supreme Court set aside the High Court order and Order-in-Original.

whyItMatters: Gadiya extends Pooja Ramesh Singh from tribunal judgments to an executive customs adjudication. The Supreme Court did not resolve the customs merits; it set aside a ₹425.28 crore penalty because fake and misused authorities entered the reasoning. That makes it part of India's unusual cluster in which the faulty AI material appears in the adjudicator's own order, alongside Buckeye Trust, KMG Wires, Sammaan Capital and Pooja Ramesh Singh. The remand to a different officer and the note to the appointing authority make the remedy institutional as well as case-specific.
practiceNote: An adjudicator using AI as research help should keep the decision-making role with the officer. Before issuing an order, every judgment, article and quoted ratio should be checked in an official database and in the source text. If a cited case exists, verify that it supports the stated ratio; if it does not, remove or rewrite the reasoning.

conduct: Self-represented criminal appellant Cody Presti relied on 95 cases in his opening brief. courtSaid.quote: The remaining eleven cases either do not exist or lacked sufficient indicia for this court to locate the authority.
In these instances, the relied upon authority simply does not exist.
We pause to note that Presti's Opening Brief is just the next example of the alarming rise of citations to fake cases by attorneys and self-represented litigants in this jurisdiction and nationally.
But that right does not authorize a defendant to cite to nonexistent authority that cannot aid their ability to present a "complete defense."

timeline.event: Presti elected to proceed self-represented in circuit court.
Circuit Court entered judgment of conviction and sentence on Count 2.
Intermediate Court of Appeals affirmed and addressed the non-existent authorities.

whyItMatters: Presti adds a criminal-appellant record to a pattern mostly built from civil sanctions. The Hawaii court identified extensive fake or unusable authority but declined to import civil Rule 11 into a direct criminal appeal by a self-represented defendant. That limits the sanction response while preserving the verification norm: the court treated arguments backed by nonexistent authority as waived and affirmed the conviction. Compared with Keaau Development and Bryan, the same state's civil and family cases, the constitutional setting changed the remedy.
practiceNote: A self-represented criminal appellant should use citations that uniquely identify a real case: full case name, reporter, page, court, and year. Before filing, search the official reporter, Westlaw/Lexis if available, or the court website, then read the passage relied on. If the case cannot be found or names a different decision, do not cite it.

caseName: Booker v. The Kroger Co., No. 1:26-cv-02006-SDG (N.D. Ga.)
court: US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, Atlanta Division
conduct: Plaintiff's counsel Christopher Johnson cited four authorities that were nonexistent or misrepresented. At the show-cause hearing he denied using AI, which the court found lacked credibility and was evasive, and he devoted half of his written response to attacking opposing counsel.

sources.label: Booker v. The Kroger Co., No. 1:26-cv-02006-SDG, ECF 66 (N.D. Ga. 28 Aug 2026), sanctions order (CourtListener RECAP)
CourtListener docket

summary: The US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia fined employment plaintiff's lawyer Christopher Johnson USD 8,000, payable to the court's sanctions fund, for citing four nonexistent or misrepresented authorities. Judge Grimberg found his show-cause response evasive and an attempt to shift blame to opposing counsel, required proof of ethics and technology CLE, and reserved further sanctions.
fabricated: four purported cases highlighted in ECF 53 — the sanctions order described them as fake, false, and misleading but did not list their names
misrepresentations of the content of real case authorities in plaintiff's filings — the sanctions order did not enumerate each authority

courtSaid.quote: This matter is before the Court on its previous Order to Show Cause [ECF 53] directed to counsel for Plaintiff to explain why he should not be sanctioned for using fake or hallucinated case authorities, as well as misrepresenting the content of real case authorities, in his filings with the Court.

Because Plaintiff’s counsel, as an officer of the Court, deliberately lied to this Court about his artificial intelligence (AI) use and because Plaintiff’s counsel’s response to the Order to Show Cause [ECF 58] lacks credibility, is evasive, and seeks to divert accountability from his own misconduct, sanctions are warranted.
You can use whatever AI tools you like, but only human beings will be held responsible for the outcome.
The Court’s Order to Show Cause highlighted four purported cases cited by Plaintiff’s counsel that represented the most egregious examples of fake, false, and misleading case authorities.

timeline.event: At the hearing, counsel denied using AI tools to prepare briefs.
Counsel’s show-cause response acknowledged that he consulted AI tools.
Court imposed an $8,000 fine and ordered CLE documentation.

whyItMatters: Booker adds a stronger culpability finding than most hallucinated-authority orders. Unlike Mata v Avianca, where the sanction targeted invented cases and post-challenge persistence, this order doubled a per-authority fine because the court found counsel lied when asked about AI use. It also enforced a standing order that allowed AI but placed responsibility on human filers. Compared with Williams v DFW Airport Board, decided one day earlier, Booker moved beyond warning to a court-registry fine and required proof of ethics and technology CLE.
practiceNote: If a judge asks whether AI tools were used, answer directly and correct any earlier filing at once. Before filing, verify each authority and each proposition against a primary legal source. A standing order that permits AI still leaves the lawyer responsible for every factual and legal error in the filed paper.

caseName: Noble v. WMC Mortgage Corp., 2026 IL App (1st) 251168-U
court: Appellate Court of Illinois, First District
conduct: Self-represented appellant Sanja Noble cited Ferguson v. Georges, 389 Ill. App. 3d 543, for the standard of review. The court found the citation led to People v. Mott instead and described it as a hallucinated citation that can occur when AI-generated responses are not verified.

sources.label: Noble v. WMC Mortgage Corp., 2026 IL App (1st) 251168-U (28 Aug 2026), order PDF via Charlotin database

summary: In Illinois, self-represented litigant Sanja Noble's mortgage appeal brief included a hallucinated citation to Ferguson v. Georges for the standard of review. The Appellate Court found the citation actually led to People v. Mott, declined to strike the brief, disregarded unsupported assertions and affirmed denial of her petition.
fabricated: Ferguson v. Georges, 389 Ill. App. 3d 543, 553-54 (2010) — citation actually appeared within People v. Mott, 389 Ill. App. 3d 539 (2009), and did not address the standard of review

courtSaid.quote: Noble’s brief contains only conclusory statements for those issues she chose to address, but no argument directly related to the denial of her section 2-1401 petition.
We also note that Noble’s brief contains a “hallucinated” citation on page 10, which occurs when AI-generated responses are used and not verified.
Thus, we decline to strike plaintiff’s brief and will not dismiss the appeal.

timeline.event: SQD Revocable Living Trust filed a pro se verified complaint.
Circuit court denied Noble leave to file a second amended complaint with prejudice.
Noble moved for leave to file a third amended complaint.
Circuit court denied Noble’s section 2-1401 petition.
Noble filed a notice of appeal.
Appellate court affirmed and identified the hallucinated citation.

whyItMatters: Noble adds an Illinois appellate example involving a self-represented appellant, not counsel. Unlike Mata v Avianca and Booker v Kroger, the court did not impose money sanctions or strike the filing. It treated the fake cite as one defect in a broader Rule 341 problem and decided the appeal because the issues and opposing brief made review possible. The order is useful because it names the verification failure in a pro se mortgage appeal and connects Illinois appellate briefing rules with AI hallucinations without creating a per se dismissal rule.
practiceNote: Before filing an Illinois appellate brief, verify every cited case in an official reporter or a recognised legal database, then confirm the cited pages support the exact standard of review. Pro se status does not relax Rule 341(h)(7). Unsupported assertions should be removed or tied to record citations and real authority before filing.

whyItMatters: Adams is a Colorado federal counterpart to Salloum’s same-day state appellate warning, but the sanction rested on counsel’s broader rule compliance problems as well as bad citations. The order is narrower than Booker because the court did not find an admitted AI denial; it said the source of misstatements was unclear. Its record value is that one phantom case triggered scrutiny of briefing, courthouse-photo rules and practice standards, ending in a $1,000 sanction payable by counsel.
practiceNote: Counsel should not delegate filing review without a final citation audit under their own name. For each authority, keep a copy or database link, confirm the quoted language and holding, and check local rules before the hearing. If the court requests a cited case, produce it immediately or correct the filing.

courtSaid.quote: Plaintiff’s submission cites two authorities that do not exist as cited.

timeline.event: PIVOT Plan later became part of the metadata and native-file discovery dispute.

whyItMatters: Ashmeade adds a pro se discovery-order example from the same district that produced Mata v Avianca. The false citations did not decide the discovery disputes, and the court still resolved the requests. The order is useful because it states the Rule 11 duty in plain terms for an unrepresented party: AI-assisted work may be used, but cited authorities must exist and support the point offered. It also shows the court distinguishing a real, possibly relevant case from the nonexistent citation actually filed.
practiceNote: For discovery letters, verify even short case citations before filing. Match the caption, docket number, reporter or Westlaw citation, date and holding. If AI points to a similar real case, cite the real case accurately and explain its relevance instead of filing a mismatched citation.

whyItMatters: James broadens the tracker beyond fake cases to AI-generated factual allegations in a pleading. Unlike Mata v Avianca, Parnell and Akerlund, the disputed material was not legal authority but police-training publications used to support a Monell theory. The report recommended denying the Rule 11 motion because the safe-harbor step failed, yet still recommended referral of every lawyer who signed the complaint. That split outcome is useful because it separates procedural defects in a sanctions motion from counsel's independent duty to verify facts.
practiceNote: Before pleading a Monell training theory, obtain the training materials or written confirmation from the issuing body. Alleging documents on information and belief does not excuse an AI-generated description that cannot be verified. If later discovery shows the material is false, amend promptly and stop relying on it.

court: Superior Court of Pennsylvania

summary: In Pennsylvania, counsel for Paige and Ty Kiser cited a non-existent Superior Court decision, Com. v. Reid, for an appellate issue in a consumer dispute. fabricated: Com v. Reid, 770 A.2d 771 (Pa. Super. 2001) — the Superior Court could find no such case; the citation led to Commonwealth v. Burton, 770 A.2d 771 (Pa. Super. 1999)

Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Prods., Inc., 530 U.S. 133, 147 (2000) — the brief attributed the majority opinion to Justice Scalia; the court said it was delivered by Justice O’Connor and did not apply

courtSaid.quote: To the extent Appellant intended to rely on a case cited to as “Com v. Reid, 770 A.2d 771 (Pa. Super. 2001), this Court can find no such case in existence.
As this section of Appellants’ brief is underdeveloped, and supported in part by non-existent or unlocatable precedent, we find the issue presented therein is waived.

Further, in light of this unlocatable precedent, “this Court is left to guess whether this counterfeit authority is the product of a chatbot, or if there is a more nefarious explanation for the misinformation.”

timeline.event: Appellants purchased the Jeep from DeSimone.
Judgment entered after the trial court granted DeSimone's compulsory nonsuit.
Superior Court found Com v. Reid unlocatable, treated the issue as waived, and affirmed.

whyItMatters: Kiser adds a state-appellate example where false authority did not lead to a money sanction. The Superior Court used the counterfeit case as part of a waiver analysis, treating the affected issue as underdeveloped rather than opening a separate sanctions track. Unlike Mata v Avianca, the filing did not include fabricated opinions or a second submission defending them. The harm was still procedural: a brief asked an appellate court to infer an evidentiary rule from a case that could not be found, and a separate misattribution of Reeves left another argument impaired.
practiceNote: For Pennsylvania appellate work, cite-checking must go beyond confirming that a volume and page exist. Counsel should open each authority, confirm the caption, court, year, author if relevant, and holding, then tie it to the argument required by Pa.R.A.P. 2119(a). A mismatched citation like Burton/Reid should be removed before filing, not left for the court to resolve.

six propositions attributed to existing cases — the court said the cases did not support them, including three propositions attributed to Edelstein v. City and County of San Francisco (2002) 29 Cal.4th 164, 171-172

courtSaid.quote: the Varmas’ opening brief contained citations to cases that do not exist, citations to cases that do not stand for the proposition cited, and quotations that do not appear in the authorities cited.

Like attorneys, pro se litigants are free to use generative AI to assist in drafting briefs but must check every citation to ensure that the cited authority exists, that it supports the proposition for which it is cited, and that quotations are accurate.

The Varmas do not deny that their brief contained the citations to four nonexistent cases, the seven fabricated quotations, and the six unsupported propositions that we identified in the order to show cause.
As self-represented litigants who signed the brief, the Varmas were solely and exclusively responsible for the contents of the brief.

timeline.event: Trial court denied the petition for entry of default administrative judgment and damages.
California Supreme Court denied review after writ denial.
Varmas filed the notice of appeal.
Varmas filed a new opening brief after the first was struck.
Varmas filed the corrected opening brief signed by both appellants.
Court issued tentative opinion warning about fabricated authority.
Court affirmed, imposed appellate-fee sanctions and referred possible unauthorized practice.

whyItMatters: Varma extends California’s AI-authority sanctions beyond lawyers to self-represented appellants who signed a brief prepared with outside help. Unlike Noland, which imposed a fixed $10,000 sanction on counsel, this opinion ordered the pro se appellants to pay the respondent’s appellate attorney fees and sent the opinion to the State Bar over possible unauthorized practice by the nonlawyer drafter. The detail on identical language across related appeals also shows how one AI-generated brief template can affect several cases.
practiceNote: A self-represented appellant who uses drafting help must still verify the brief line by line before signing it. Check that each case exists, each quotation appears in the cited opinion and each cited holding supports the proposition. If a tentative opinion flags fabricated authority, move promptly to withdraw or correct the brief.

caseName: Williams v. Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport Board, No. 4:26-cv-00433-P (N.D. Tex.)
court: US District Court, Northern District of Texas
conduct: Plaintiffs' counsel relied on nonexistent and out-of-circuit cases while trying to establish clearly established law in a civil-rights action. summary: In the Northern District of Texas, plaintiffs' counsel cited nonexistent and materially inapposite cases while trying to defeat qualified immunity. Judge Pittman called the effort borderline sanctionable, warned that generative-AI misrepresentations of law may trigger Rule 11 sanctions, and dismissed the civil-rights claims against the airport-board defendants.
fabricated: Iko v. Shreve, 122 F.3d 707 (4th Cir. 1997) — either nonexistent or mistakenly out-of-circuit and inapposite; the court said plaintiffs presumably meant Iko v. Shreve, 535 F.3d 225 (4th Cir. 2008)
Yates v. Terry, 817 F.3d 877 (4th Cir. 2016) — out-of-circuit and materially dissimilar
Dawkins v. Fields 354 F.3d 392 (5th Cir. 2003) — the court could not find a case clearly establishing the point
Tennessee v. Garner, 471 U.S. 1 (1985) — misused to argue non-deadly force against a compliant, non-threatening person is unreasonable
Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386 (1989) — did not clearly establish law for a single taser discharge against a non-compliant adult

courtSaid.quote: This cannot be undertaken at too broad a level of generality, id., and it certainly cannot be established by citation to nonexistent cases.
Here, Plaintiffs make a borderline sanctionable attempt to identify “clearly established” law from five cases.
The Court cautions that use of generative artificial intelligence that results in repeated misrepresentations of law may qualify for sanctions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)–(c)

Plaintiffs filed the civil-rights suit.
Defendants filed the motion to dismiss addressed by the order.

whyItMatters: Williams adds a qualified-immunity setting in which weak citation practice directly affected the clearly established law inquiry. Unlike Booker, the court issued a warning rather than a fine, but it linked hallucinated authority to Rule 11 because the plaintiff's burden required a close match to binding precedent. The record also shows a separate risk from AI research: even real out-of-circuit cases, or real Supreme Court cases stated at too high a level, cannot satisfy the Fifth Circuit standard.
practiceNote: When opposing qualified immunity, build a table before filing: jurisdiction, facts, force used, procedural posture and holding for each case. Verify the reporter citation and court. Remove out-of-circuit cases unless they are used only for persuasive background, and do not cite broad Supreme Court excessive-force language as if it clearly establishes the precise conduct.

Unlike Mezu v Mezu, the court did not refer the litigant or impose money sanctions, partly because the case was being dismissed in full. practiceNote: A self-represented party still needs a cite-check process before filing. Search the caption, docket number, reporter citation and Westlaw citation in a legal database. Some specific statutory references were also inaccurate. For example, a reference was made to evidence satisfying section 24 of the NDIS Act, which addresses the disability requirements for meeting the access criteria of the NDIS and is no application here given MFRD’s status as an existing participant in the NDIS, who has already met the access criteria.

The practice direction continues on to note that the presentation of false and inaccurate information to the Tribunal is unacceptable and may hamper the Tribunal achieving its objectives and making the correct or preferable decision in a proceeding.

Mr A lodged an AAT review application for MFRD.

The Tribunal accepted that the tool misled a non-lawyer, but still recorded the practical cost: sections of the submission had to be disregarded or treated with caution. That mix shows why Australian tribunal practice directions focus on disclosure and verification rather than treating every AI error as a disciplinary event.
practiceNote: For ART and NDIS matters, a representative using generative AI should check each case name, citation, jurisdiction and statutory section before filing. The check must include whether the case is about the NDIS and whether the cited section applies to the participant’s status. Where the ART practice direction applies, the party should also follow its filing responsibilities for AI-assisted documents.

summary: In Maryland, appellate counsel filed a criminal brief with multiple inaccurate citations. Here, counsel for appellant has not admitted that the mistakes in the brief were due to the use of AI, but that seems likely.

In this case, however, the brief was filed before the decision in Mezu, the inaccuracies were not excessive and did not include totally made up cases, counsel tried to correct the errors before the State filed its brief, and the State does not contend that it was harmed.

the Court identified “three other briefs [that] contain similar errors” and ordered Ms. Tate to address those “additional examples [that] may also be attributable to the misuse of generative AI.”

whyItMatters: Ruiz extends the tracker's Arizona federal-court line from fake case citations to false direct quotations in otherwise real authorities. Unlike Mata v Avianca, the court found remorse and no dishonest motive, yet still treated repeated quotation errors across four filings as public discipline. The order also follows McCarthy v DEA and Malkeet Lnu v Blanche in treating a lawyer's cite-check process as insufficient when the lawyer asks an AI tool to produce a list of cases rather than checking each proposition in the filed brief. The sanction was not monetary, but it created a reportable reprimand and left any State Bar referral unresolved in the record.
practiceNote: A lawyer who uses AI to draft must verify each quotation and statutory excerpt against the filed brief, not against an AI-generated case list. For every quoted phrase, open the official opinion or statute, confirm the exact words, and remove quotation marks if the language is only a paraphrase. The signing lawyer should keep the checked text with the filing record.

courtSaid.quote: את התגובה לתשובה לבקשת האישור ביסס ב"כ המבקש בין היתר על "הזיות AI", היינו הפניות לאסמכתאות שנחזות להיראות כפסקי דין אף כי בפועל לא היו ולא נבראו.
בחנתי את הדברים תוך עיון בהפניות לאסמכתאות המיומרות שבתגובה לתשובה לבקשת האישור אשר כשלעצמה נחזית להיראות כאילו נערכה באופן חפוז ומרושל, או באמצעות בינה מלאכותית ללא ראשית ראשיתה של בדיקה ועריכה.
שקלתי ולא פסקתי כך לא בלי היסוס. אסתפק בהתראה ובהדגשת הזהירות הנדרשת בערי כת כתבי טענות ובהסתייעות באמצעי בינה מלאכותית לצורך עריכתם.
המבקש יישא בהוצאות המשיבה בסך ₪ 20,000

timeline.event: Capital Markets Authority circular 2019-9-7 on institutional call-centre waiting times was published.
Circular 2019-9-7 came into force, setting the waiting-time framework at issue.
Pretrial hearing addressed the application and AIG's AI-hallucination objection.
Withdrawal approved; the personal claim was dismissed and applicant ordered to pay ₪20,000 costs.

whyItMatters: Adibi is one of the folder's three Israeli records but differs from Ben Cohen v Municipality of Ramat Gan, where a public body used fabricated sources. Here the source says a class-action applicant's response relied on non-existent consumer authorities, and the court considered but did not impose personal costs against counsel. The monetary order in the decision was ₪20,000 costs against the applicant after withdrawal, in addition to a warning about uncontrolled AI use in representative proceedings. That matters because adequacy of representation is central to class actions; unreliable authorities can affect both the merits filter and the lawyer's ability to act for absent class members.
practiceNote: In Israeli class actions, counsel should verify every authority in the response to answer before oral argument, including docket number, court, date and location in Nevo or the official court database. If the case cannot be found or the source lacks a citation, remove it and tell the court before the opponent has to raise the issue. Counsel should also check that the cited rule addresses the class-certification element being argued.

caseName: Capital Standard, LLC v. U.S. Bank National Association, No. 2D2024-1392 (Fla. 2d DCA)
court: Florida Second District Court of Appeal
conduct: Attorney Kenneth H. Keefe's amended initial brief contained at least 31 instances of hallucinated or misrepresented authority, including a fake quotation attributed to Hart Properties v. Slack, and the problems continued after a January 2026 show-cause order.

regulatoryOutcome.disposition: Court referred counsel to The Florida Bar. No disposition on record.

sources.label: Capital Standard, LLC v. U.S. Bank N.A., No. 2D2024-1392 (Fla. 2d DCA 21 Aug 2026), opinion (Florida Courts)
CourtListener opinion

summary: Florida's Second District Court of Appeal affirmed a foreclosure-related declaratory judgment and, in a separate section citing the Charlotin database, fined appellant's counsel USD 1,500, awarded U.S. Bank its appellate fees, and referred him to The Florida Bar for rampant hallucinated citations that persisted after a show-cause order. Counsel may not bill his client for either amount.
fabricated: Maciejewski v. Holland, 441 So. 2d 703 (Fla. 2d DCA 1983) — cited for ratification and transaction-validity propositions the opinion does not contain
Hart Properties, Inc. v. Slack, 159 So. 2d 236, 239 (Fla. 1963) — nonexistent quotation on fundamental error
Miami Country Day School v. Bakst, 641 So. 2d 467 (Fla. 3d DCA 1994) — cited for bona-fide purchaser and delay-bar propositions the opinion does not contain
Gonzalez v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co., 95 So. 3d 251 (Fla. 2d DCA 2012) — cited as authority on possession presumptions and bona fide purchaser status; the case concerns assignment standing
Board of Regents v. Wilson, 365 So. 2d 213 (Fla. 1st DCA 1979) — fake case
Forty-six total hallucinations in the amended initial brief and reply brief — the court did not enumerate all forty-six

courtSaid.quote: Capital Standard's subsequent amended initial brief included at least thirty-one instances of Attorney Keefe's citing or quoting existing cases for propositions they do not contain.
Capital Standard's reply brief added another fifteen AI hallucinations, including the fake case Board of Regents v. Wilson, 365 So. 2d 213 (Fla. 1st DCA 1979);
Rather, it is his use of generative AI without also "ensur[ing] that the legal propositions and authority generated are trustworthy."

In conclusion, we impose on Attorney Keefe a $1,500 fine payable to the clerk of this court within fourteen days; we remand this matter to the trial court to determine the reasonable amount of appellate attorney's fees incurred by U.S. Bank for researching and answering Capital Standard's amended initial brief; and we refer Attorney Keefe to The Florida Bar for further proceedings.

timeline.event: Court issued a show-cause order identifying forty-six hallucinations.
Court struck the amended initial and reply briefs and directed counsel to notify clients.
Attorney Keefe responded, saying he had used AI as a supplemental research tool.
Florida's signature-rule amendment made existence and accuracy of cited authorities an express filing representation.
Opinion affirmed judgment, imposed $1,500 fine, fee remand and Bar referral.

whyItMatters: Capital Standard shows a state appellate court moving past warnings in Florida AI-citation cases. The opinion cites Rangel, Goya and Gutierrez, then adds a fine, a personal fee award and a Florida Bar referral after counsel missed a show-cause deadline and left forty-six hallucinations in the amended and reply briefs. Unlike Mata v Avianca, the court was not dealing with invented opinions attached to a trial motion, but with appellate merits briefing that the panel said was almost wholly untrustworthy. The opinion also ties the sanction to Florida's June 2026 signature-rule amendment, making cite verification an express certification in future filings.
practiceNote: Before filing an appeal brief in Florida, the signer should read each authority and match every proposition to a page or paragraph. A separate table of citation, proposition and source text would have answered the January 8 order. If any authority cannot be verified, the brief should be amended before filing and the client told promptly if a court raises the issue.

caseName: Disruptive Resources, LLC v. Ballistic Barrier Products Inc., No. 1:24-cv-00321-JCG (D. Del.)
court: US District Court for the District of Delaware (Judge Jennifer Choe-Groves, sitting by designation)
conduct: Plaintiff's counsel self-disclosed that a joint claim-construction brief prepared with the AI tool Strongsuit, used to generate an outline and pull deposition statements, contained multiple AI-induced errors, including a claim-construction position contrary to his own client's.

sources.label: Disruptive Resources, LLC v. Ballistic Barrier Products Inc., D.I. 115 (D. Del. 20 Aug 2026), order discharging show cause (CourtListener RECAP)
Volokh Conspiracy, 25 Aug 2026 (secondary)

summary: In a patent case in the US District Court for the District of Delaware, plaintiff's counsel promptly disclosed that a Strongsuit-assisted claim-construction brief contained errors. Judge Jennifer Choe-Groves discharged the show-cause order without Rule 11 sanctions, distinguishing lawyers who defend hallucinations from those who self-report, while warning that future AI mistakes in the case would be sanctioned.
fabricated: Portions of Plaintiff's claim-construction reply brief — erroneously proposed construction deviated from Plaintiff's own construction
Two sections of the Joint Claim Construction Brief — concluding statements proposed incorrect claim constructions; the court did not list the claim terms
A third section of the Joint Claim Construction Brief — withdrawn entirely because it contained more pervasive errors; the court did not list the errors

courtSaid.quote: After Plaintiff’s counsel disclosed to the Court that the previously filed Joint Claim Construction Brief (“Joint Brief”) (D.I. 105) featured multiple errors due to his use of generative artificial intelligence (“AI”), the Court ordered counsel to show cause in writing as to why the Court should not impose sanctions for counsel’s conduct pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b),(c).

The Court observes that the Joint Letter identified that two sections of the Joint Brief contained a concluding statement that proposed an incorrect claim construction, and a third section was withdrawn entirely because it “contained more pervasive errors.”
In this case, counsel took full responsibility for his mistakes, was not evasive, and prioritized candor to the Court and opposing counsel by disclosing the errors quickly.
The Court warns counsel that any future incidents involving AI mistakes in this case may result in sanctions.

timeline.event: Counsel filed a letter describing disclosure of AI-attributable inaccuracies.
Court held a hearing on counsel's AI errors.
Court declined sanctions and warned that future AI mistakes may be sanctioned.

whyItMatters: Disruptive Resources differs from citation-hallucination records such as Mata v Avianca and Ruiz v Magellan. The problem was not a fake case, but AI-drafted patent claim-construction text that took positions contrary to the client's case. The court credited prompt disclosure, full responsibility and candor to the opponent, then declined Rule 11 sanctions while warning that another AI mistake in the same case may be sanctioned. The record is therefore a counterpoint: courts may distinguish a lawyer who self-reports and cures AI drafting errors from one who defends false authorities, but they still treat unreviewed AI output as a Rule 11 risk.
practiceNote: For AI-assisted claim-construction briefs, counsel should compare each proposed construction in the filed draft against the party's served constructions and expert record before filing. A final whole-brief read is needed; section-by-section edits are not enough. If an error is filed, notify opposing counsel and the court promptly and propose a clean amended brief.

caseName: Faiz Enterprise v. State Tax Officer, Unit-67, Surat, R/SCA No. 10123 of 2026 (Gujarat High Court)
court: High Court of Gujarat
conduct: A GST registration-cancellation order cited State of Gujarat v. Aarbee Structures 2024 (4) TMI 951, which does not exist, and misattributed Sri Vinayaga Agencies and Jyoti Tar Products. The state tax officer admitted having used an AI tool.

sources.label: Faiz Enterprise v. State Tax Officer, R/SCA No. 10123 of 2026 (Gujarat HC 20 Aug 2026), order (Charlotin database archive PDF)

summary: The High Court of Gujarat quashed a GST registration-cancellation order after finding that the state tax officer had relied on AI-generated, nonexistent and misattributed case law. After the officer admitted using AI, the court laid down verification instructions for all tax officers and warned that future breaches may attract disciplinary action and amount to contempt of court.
fabricated: State of Gujarat v. Aarbee Structures Pvt. Ltd., 2024 (4) TMI 951 — not in existence
M/s. Sri Vinayaga Agencies v. Assistant Commissioner, 2023 (5) TMI 106 — different citation and ratio did not apply
Jyoti Tar Products Pvt. Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner, 2024 (7) TMI 512 — did not match any citation and ratio did not apply

courtSaid.quote: It appears that the impugned order has been passed by the State Tax Officer by placing reliance exclusively on the AI generated case laws.

The affidavit-in-reply (tendering unconditional apology), specifically refers that the deponent is a probationary officer and due to his lack of experience, the mistake has happened and he has tendered unconditional apology to this Court for using the Artificial Intelligence (AI) in drafting the order and referring to the non-existent and irrelevant judgments.

Any case law, statutory provision, rule, circular, notification identified through AI must be independently verified by the Authority using primary official sources before incorporating it in an order.
Failure to follow these instructions, including passing orders based on unverified AI content, will amount to misconduct and may attract disciplinary action.

timeline.event: Show-cause notice issued to the taxpayer.
GST registration cancellation order passed with nonexistent or irrelevant AI-generated case law.
Revocation application rejected; the order issued on 2026-03-23.
Appellate order passed; GST APL-04 issued on 2026-05-26.
High Court order flagged the cited authorities and required instructions.
Additional Commissioner issued statewide AI-use instructions for tax authorities.
High Court quashed the notice and orders and directed fresh proceedings.

whyItMatters: Faiz Enterprise adds a non-lawyer public decision-maker to India's records. Unlike Sammaan Capital v Mantri, where fabricated Supreme Court cases appeared in a judge's order and no AI tool was identified, the state tax officer admitted AI use and the High Court obtained department-wide instructions within five days. It also differs from Pooja Ramesh Singh v JK Bank because the faulty authority sat inside an administrative GST cancellation chain before judicial review. The remedy was operational as well as case-specific: the taxpayer received a fresh notice, and all Gujarat tax adjudicators were told that unverified AI content may be misconduct and contempt.
practiceNote: A tax officer using AI for draft orders must locate each cited judgment in an official database, check its citation and legal status, and paste the relevant paragraph before relying on it. The officer should also address the taxpayer's cited cases with reasons. After Faiz Enterprise, ignoring those checks in Gujarat risks misconduct findings and contempt.

caseName: Full Standard Properties v. SJ 6070, No. 5:25-cv-09451 (N.D. Cal.)
court: US District Court for the Northern District of California
conduct: Plaintiff's counsel cited nonexistent cases in filings. Before the show-cause hearing counsel had reimbursed USD 14,500 in attorney's fees that the fabricated citations caused the opposing party to incur; the order to show cause was then discharged. The court's total fee award in the matter was USD 85,980.70.

sources.label: Full Standard Properties v. SJ 6070, No. 5:25-cv-09451, ECF 41 (N.D. Cal. 20 Aug 2026), order (CourtListener RECAP)

summary: In the US District Court for the Northern District of California, Judge Freeman discharged an order to show cause against plaintiff's counsel who had cited nonexistent cases, after counsel reimbursed USD 14,500 in fees the fabricated citations had caused the opposing party. The court's overall fee award in the matter was USD 85,980.70.
fabricated: Multiple citations to nonexistent cases in Plaintiff's ECF 18 opposition — the court did not identify the case names
Pin citations to real cases in Plaintiff's ECF 18 opposition — pages were not in the cited case or discussed issues unrelated to Defendant's fee motion

courtSaid.quote: Plaintiff filed a brief containing multiple citations to nonexistent cases.
Where the opposition brief identifies cases that do exist, the pin citations are to pages that are not contained within the case or that discuss issues having no bearing on Defendant’s motion.
The parties have resolved that issue informally, and Plaintiff’s counsel has reimbursed Defendant for attorneys’ fees in the amount of $14,500.
The Order to Show Cause issued on May 21, 2026 (ECF 30) is DISCHARGED.

timeline.event: Plaintiff filed the state-court action over the foreclosure.
Court ordered plaintiff's counsel to show cause over nonexistent cases in the fee opposition.
Counsel's written response to the show-cause order was due.
Court discharged the show-cause order after counsel reimbursed $14,500.
Court awarded defendant $85,980.70 in fees, subject to the $14,500 setoff.

whyItMatters: Full Standard is a sanctions-light federal record. Unlike Capital Standard v U.S. Bank, the court did not publish the fabricated authorities or refer counsel after the reimbursement. The order still shows a practical cost path: counsel who caused an opponent to research nonexistent authorities paid the opponent's response costs before sanctions were decided, and the show-cause order was discharged. That makes it useful alongside Mata v Avianca because the remedy targeted wasted fee-briefing work rather than punishing the client or changing the merits outcome. The case also shows why public records may undercount hallucination details when the parties resolve sanctions informally.
practiceNote: When an opponent moves for fees, every cited case and pin cite in the response should be checked against the reporter page before filing. If false authorities are discovered after filing, counsel should disclose them, reimburse costs caused by the error where appropriate, and replace the filing with verified citations before a show-cause hearing.

caseName: Yunes v. M.A. Asli Marketing, Case 7669-06-24 (Haifa Regional Labor Court)
court: Haifa Regional Labor Court

sources.label: Yunes v. M.A. Asli Marketing, 7669-06-24 (Haifa Regional Labor Court, 17 Aug 2026), decision in Hebrew (Charlotin database archive PDF)

summary: In an employment claim before the Haifa Regional Labor Court in Israel, the court found that several precedents cited by the worker's lawyer did not exist. CA 407/89 Tzuk Or Ltd. v. Car Security Ltd., PD 48(5) 661 (1994) — a real case, but the quoted passage on linked-company debts does not appear in it

לא עלה בידו לאתר את הפסיקה הנ"ל אשר "הובאה במסגרת הבקשה תיקון כתב התביעה וככול הנראה מקורה במידע שנמסר מחיפוש במערכות בינה מלאכותית, שהח"מ סמך את ידו עליה ולא עלה בדעתו לאמתו בדרך אחרת"
בית הדין רואה בחומרה רבה את התנהלות ב"כ התובע אשר הביא פסיקה וציטוטים שאינם קיימים
לאור התנהלות ב"כ התובע אשר "עשה שימוש בבינה מלאכותית אשר הניב פסקי דין ש אינם קיימים וציטוטים שלא היו ולא נבראו" - יישא התובע בהוצאות בסך ₪ 4,000 לטובת אוצר המדינה.

timeline.event: Worker filed the labour claim.
Plaintiff filed summaries citing labour and civil precedents.
Court said it could not locate two cited judgments and requested copies.
Counsel said he could not locate them and they likely came from an AI search.
Court struck claims against defendants 4-7 and ordered ₪6,000 total costs.

whyItMatters: Yunes gives the tracker a labour-court example from Israel, different from Adibi's class-action withdrawal and Ben Cohen's public-body filing. The fabricated material affected jurisdiction and veil-piercing arguments in an employment claim rather than a consumer or administrative matter. The court also used a split costs response: ₪2,000 to defendants 4-7 for the dismissed claims and ₪4,000 to the state treasury because counsel used AI that produced nonexistent cases and quotations. The source therefore shows how a court can sanction AI citation misuse even while leaving part of the labour case alive against shareholder defendants.
practiceNote: Before filing summaries, counsel should search each Israeli labour or civil citation in Nevo or the official court database and save the full judgment. If the court asks for copies, counsel should either produce the source or withdraw the citation at once. For veil-piercing arguments, use authorities that match the defendant's shareholder status and the labour court's jurisdiction.

caseName: Guerra-Quezada v. United States (with Guerra-Vasquez v. United States), Nos. 25-10372 and 25-10555 (5th Cir.)
court: US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
conduct: Appellants' counsel quoted Ng Fung Ho v. White for language found in no opinion, cited Doe v. McAleenan as a Fourth Circuit case when it is a Seventh Circuit decision, and misattributed a Perez v. Brownell dissent to Afroyim v. Rusk.

sources.label: Guerra-Quezada v. United States, Nos. 25-10372, 25-10555, Doc. 71-1 (5th Cir. 14 Aug 2026), opinion (Charlotin database archive PDF)

summary: In consolidated appeals by an uncle and nephew claiming US citizenship, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit identified fabricated quotations and misattributed authorities in both briefs, including language attributed to Ng Fung Ho v. White found in no opinion. It treated the affected arguments as forfeited and warned counsel that FRAP 28 prohibits citing nonexistent authority.
fabricated: Ng Fung Ho v. White, 259 U.S. 276, 284 (1922) — purported quotation “[N]o deportable alien may be expelled until it has first been determined . . . that he is in fact an alien” was not located in Ng Fung Ho or any other opinion
Ng Fung Ho v. White, 259 U.S. 276 (1922) — phrase “[i]t is wrong to deport a United States citizen” does not appear in the opinion
Guerra-Vasquez opening brief parenthetical to Ng Fung Ho — cited the correct part but misquoted the majority
Doe v. McAleenan, 926 F.3d 910 (7th Cir. 2019) — cited as a Fourth Circuit opinion starting on a different Federal Reporter page
Afroyim v. Rusk, 387 U.S. 253 (1967) — quote actually came from Perez v. Brownell, 356 U.S. 44, 64 (1958) (Warren, C.J., dissenting)

courtSaid.quote: They are completely unsubstantiated by citations to the record, and the case citations in the briefing are systematically defective.
This court’s research has failed to locate this quote in Ng Fung Ho or in any other opinion.
Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 28 requires all filed briefs to contain arguments supported by “citations to the authorities,” disallowing citation to nonexistent or fabricated cases.
The court takes no action now for the foregoing deficiencies, but counsel must take this obligation seriously in the future.

timeline.event: Fifth Circuit filed its opinion in the consolidated appeals.
Panel treated due-process arguments as forfeited because record and case citations were defective.
Panel identified fabricated Ng Fung Ho language, Doe circuit error and Perez-Afroyim misattribution.
Panel warned counsel under FRAP 28 and 46 but took no disciplinary action.

whyItMatters: Guerra-Quezada shows the Fifth Circuit using forfeiture and warning, not a separate sanctions order, when false quotations appear inside merits briefing. Unlike Capital Standard v U.S. Bank, there was no fine or referral; unlike Ruiz v Magellan, the court did not issue a public reprimand. The opinion still records specific defects: invented Ng Fung Ho language, a circuit misidentification, and a quote moved from a Perez dissent to Afroyim. Because the disputed claims involved citizenship and removal, the citation failures affected a high-stakes appeal while the court was also deciding jurisdiction. The entry helps distinguish appellate discipline warnings from cases where courts impose monetary or professional sanctions.
practiceNote: For immigration and citizenship appeals, counsel should check every quoted sentence against the official U.S. Reports or Federal Reporter text and verify the court, page and precedential status of each citation. A quote from a dissent should be labelled as a dissent and not moved to a later majority decision. Record citations must be checked at the same time.

Court fined the plaintiff 2% of the updated claim value and ordered notice to OAB bodies.

whyItMatters: Within the Brazilian records, this São Paulo decision sits between the TJPR record and Brazil TRT-2. The court went beyond refusing to consider an AI-tainted filing; it used CPC bad-faith rules to fine the party and send the ruling to both state and federal bar bodies. The source ties the result to the OAB 2024 recommendation requiring human supervision of generative tools. That makes the record useful for tracking how Brazilian courts move from finding fake precedent to treating unsupervised AI use as a professional conduct matter.
practiceNote: Before filing in a Brazilian court, counsel should open each precedent from an official court database and save the citation check with the draft. If AI helped draft the petition, a human reviewer must confirm the existence and holding of each authority before protocolizing it. The OAB recommendation cited by the court made that supervision a professional expectation, not a post-filing option.

summary: The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal dismissed a family-law appeal for failure to perfect it and ordered lump-sum costs of CAD 20,000 after the self-represented appellant filed AI-generated transcripts containing invented testimony and a forged transcriber's certificate. Certificate of court transcriber page bearing Sue Loney's name, NS Registration Number, and signature; appended to the AI-generated transcripts without a certified transcription

courtSaid.quote: He claims the false certifications are the result of AI hallucinations and not the product of an attempt to mislead Ms. Tanner and this Court.
We now know that Mr. Arbuckle did not file a certified transcription from Videoplus or any other certified transcriptionist.

He has been non-compliant with the Rules by: (1) providing a certificate of readiness he knew was inaccurate; (2) filing an uncertified transcript on June 3, 2026; (3) filing an uncertified transcript on June 22, 2026; and (4) failing to file a compliant appeal book on the date set by the Court.

whyItMatters: Arbuckle adds a different failure mode from citation cases such as Mata v Avianca and Harber v HMRC. The AI output was not legal authority; it was the record itself. The appeal book appeared compliant because it carried a real transcriber's certification, registration number and signature, yet the transcript contained discrepancies and uncertified material. The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal treated that as harm to the appeal process, not a defect cured by another extension. practiceNote: An appellant must order transcripts from a certified court reporter before certifying readiness. Armco, Inc. v. Penrod-Stauffer Building Systems, Inc., 733 F.2d 1087, 1089 (4th Cir. 1984) — quoted only the first half of the paragraph and omitted the limiting sentence that service rules may not be ignored

courtSaid.quote: This opinion also sanctions Forney's attorney, Lucas Colantonio, for submitting a brief that contained fabricated legal authority for the second time.
There should not be a next time. If there is, the court will impose monetary and other sanctions.

Thus the record establishes by clear and convincing evidence that Colantonio knowingly submitted a pleading containing fabricated authority and citations on multiple occasions and even after being warned.

Further, the Clerk of Court is directed to send a copy of this order and a transcript of the April 16, 2026 hearing (D.E. 18) to the North Carolina State Bar for whatever action it deems appropriate, including consideration of whether disciplinary or disability-related measures are warranted.

timeline.event: Forney filed the first discrimination action against Cary.
Court dismissed Forney I and warned counsel against non-existent cases.
Forney filed the second action against Cary.
Town moved to dismiss the second complaint.

Court held a show-cause hearing on counsel’s citations.
Court recommended dismissal, ordered fee sanctions, and referred counsel.

whyItMatters: Forney is a repeat-warning record. The same lawyer had been told in Forney I that another non-existent citation would bring monetary and other sanctions, yet the second case reused the same In re S.L.L. citation and the same incomplete Armco passage. That makes it closer to Deutsche Bank v LeTennier than to first-notice cases such as In re Booker. The order is also useful because it treats failure to read the prior warning and failure to investigate the source of the first citation as aggravating facts.
practiceNote: After a court flags a false citation, the next filing should begin with a documented recheck of the prior order and every authority reused from the earlier brief. Do not rely on a replacement case named from memory at a hearing. Bring the full decision, pinpoint the page, and confirm that the unquoted part of a paragraph does not defeat the proposition.

courtSaid.quote: The most plausible explanation, certainly for the fictitious Lubbe reference, is that it is the product of the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and what has been dubbed ‘hallucinations’.
Names of non-existent cases are not law. Jumbled together quotes from cases, some identified, some not, are not law.
The sources of law, the authority for legal principle, which is what the present case touches on, must be checked before they can be used and adopted into judicial reasoning.
I intend forwarding this judgment to the Chairperson of the Legal Practice Council for an investigation.

whyItMatters: FJL is the tracker’s judge-authored false-authority record. Unlike Mavundla and Northbound Processing, the questioned material appeared in a judgment, not in counsel’s heads of argument. The full court still upheld the outcome after doing its own section 18(3) analysis, but Opperman J treated the discrepancies as a possible professional-conduct issue for an acting judge who remained an enrolled practitioner. The record matters because it separates the parties’ relief from accountability for the author of the judgment and identifies the LPC as the available forum.
practiceNote: A judgment should not be handed down until each authority and quoted passage has been checked against the law report or SAFLII. Acting judges using research help or AI need the same final source audit as counsel. If discrepancies are found after delivery, address them on the record and through the proper professional body, not by private chambers discussion.

caseName: Mendel S. v. Faigy S., 2026 NY Slip Op 26118 (Fam. Ct., Kings County)
court: Family Court of the State of New York, Kings County
conduct: Counsel, anonymised in the published opinion as 'Connor C., Esq.', filed objections in a child-support proceeding in which 11 of 16 cited authorities were fabricated and nearly all the remainder did not support the propositions cited. Counsel completed an AI-policy CLE course in response.

sources.label: Mendel S. v. Faigy S., 2026 NY Slip Op 26118 (Fam. Ct. Kings Cty. 31 Jul 2026), published opinion (Charlotin database archive PDF)

summary: A judge of the Family Court of the State of New York, Kings County, reviewing child-support objections on the court's own motion, found eleven of sixteen citations were AI-generated fictions and the rest miscited. The court imposed a USD 1,000 sanction for frivolous conduct but declined a grievance referral because counsel promptly accepted responsibility and completed AI-policy training.
fabricated: Eleven of sixteen citations in the Family Court Act § 439(e) Objection — fabricated; the opinion did not list the case names
Nearly all remaining real cases in the Objection — did not support the propositions asserted; the opinion did not list them

courtSaid.quote: Upon review of the Objection, the Court discovered that Counsel repeatedly cited “hallucinated cases”—fictitious judicial authorities generated by artificial intelligence that do not exist or do not stand for the propositions asserted.
Eleven of the sixteen citations were fabricated, and in nearly all instances, the real cases (once located by the Court) did not support the propositions for which counsel cited them.
It would have taken minimal time for counsel — and it was also his responsibility as an attorney — to check the citations on Westlaw or Lexis to determine their veracity.

The Court finds, given the facts of this case and the response filed by counsel as described above, that sanctions are appropriate, but the Court will not refer Mr. C to the Attorney Grievance Committee.

timeline.event: Court decided its sua sponte order to show cause.
Opinion found eleven of sixteen citations fabricated.
Court noted counsel’s response, citation log, CLE certificate, and letters.
Court imposed a $1,000 sanction and declined grievance referral.

whyItMatters: Mendel brings the New York hallucinated-citation line into a Family Court child-support objection. Compared with Deutsche Bank v LeTennier, the proportion of fabricated citations was high, but the response was lower because counsel promptly took responsibility, supplied a citation log, completed AI-policy CLE, and did not keep adding fake authorities after notice. The record adds a high-volume court setting: the opinion ties wasted cite-checking time to support objections that already sit on top of heavy Family Court calendars.
practiceNote: Before filing an objection under Family Court Act § 439(e), check every AI-assisted citation in Westlaw or Lexis and save the result. A post hoc citation log and AI-policy CLE may mitigate, but they do not cure the filed defect. Any response to an order to show cause should be affirmed under penalty of perjury when CPLR 2106 requires it.

caseName: TOV Realty, LLC v. Suarez; Kosel Equity, LLC v. MacGregor, No. SC21183 (Conn.)
court: Connecticut Supreme Court
aiTool: ChatGPT (used to edit briefs after Lexis research)
conduct: Attorney Ian G. Gottlieb of GLG Law filed certification applications and briefs in two public-interest landlord-tenant appeals containing about seven hallucinated citations. He had researched on Lexis, then pasted the drafts into ChatGPT for editing, which added or altered case citations. He admitted a Rule 1.1 competence violation.

regulatoryOutcome.disposition: The court ordered a courtesy copy of its sanctions order sent to the Committee and the order posted on the Judicial Branch website; no formal referral or Committee disposition on record.

sources.label: TOV Realty, LLC v. Suarez, SC21183 (Conn. 31 Jul 2026), sanctions order (Connecticut Judicial Branch)
Volokh Conspiracy, 4 Aug 2026 (secondary)

summary: The Connecticut Supreme Court sanctioned a landlord's lawyer whose Lexis-verified briefs acquired fabricated citations when he pasted them into ChatGPT for editing. It ordered six hours of CLE, USD 1,000 each from counsel and the firm to the Connecticut Bar Institute, a compliance report and a courtesy copy to the grievance committee, crediting his candour.
fabricated: Approximately seven erroneous and unverified citations in the public-interest appeal applications and briefs; the order did not enumerate each citation

courtSaid.quote: We are required to confront for the first time a lawyer’s use of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) that has resulted in the submission of written materials to this court containing citations that were “hallucinated”—in other words, fabricated or inaccurately generated.
Unbeknownst to Attorney Gottlieb, the drafts produced by ChatGPT added new case citations or altered existing case citations, making the final documents filed in this court inaccurate and misleading.

He admitted, through counsel, that he filed documents in these matters containing a total of seven erroneous and unverified citations that resulted from the use of generative AI in the editing and review process.
We emphasize that this courtesy copy is not a referral for further disciplinary action.

timeline.event: Superior Court AI verification rule, Practice Book § 4-9, took effect.
Court held the show-cause hearing over hallucinated citations.
Appellate AI rule amendments, including Practice Book § 62-6(d), took effect.
Court imposed CLE, donation, compliance-report, and courtesy-copy sanctions.

whyItMatters: TOV is the Connecticut Supreme Court’s first sanctions order for a lawyer’s generative-AI citations. It differs from Barteca and In re Booker because the original research had been checked in Lexis before ChatGPT was used as an editor, and the court found no intent to deceive. The sanction still required extra CLE, two USD 1,000 donations, a compliance report, posting on the Judicial Branch website, and a courtesy copy to the grievance committee. The record shows that editing tools can alter citations after a valid research pass.
practiceNote: Re-check citations after AI editing, even if the pre-edit draft was verified in Lexis or Shepard’s. Compare the final filed PDF against the source for every citation, quotation, and parenthetical. Connecticut filings also require compliance with Practice Book §§ 4-9 and 62-6(d), which require independent verification of AI-produced citations, authorities, and evidence.

whyItMatters: Scott is a state-appellate escalation record. Illinois had already seen Baby Boy and related Fourth District referrals with USD 1,000 fines, but the First District set a USD 1,500 rate for every false citation or quotation. The false material was not limited to cases; it included invented statutory language that became counsel’s main jurisdiction and merits theory. That makes the record a useful comparison to TOV, where the legal propositions stayed sound, and to Barteca, where the sanction turned on false case quotations in motion practice.
practiceNote: For statutory appeals, paste the operative statute and rule text from the current official source, then compare the final brief against it word for word. Every case cite needs a pinpoint to the quoted language or proposition. A show-cause response must use current statutes and pin cites too; it is not a place for another unverified AI pass.

It was intrinsic patent evidence in a claim-construction chart. The order shows that AI verification duties cover the specification, figures, prosecution history and file wrapper, not only statutes and decisions. It also records mitigation: the lawyer corrected the chart quickly, accepted responsibility and the court imposed no sanction, yet OED still used a public reprimand because the filing had been signed and submitted to a tribunal.
practiceNote: For patent filings, verify every AI-assisted citation against the intrinsic record before signing: open the patent, figures, prosecution history and file wrapper, then confirm the quoted text and pinpoint. caseName: Lichfield v. Kubler; Netflix, Inc., No. 25-4135 (10th Cir.)
court: US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
conduct: Appellant's counsel from Hepworth Legal of Bountiful, Utah, cited a nonexistent authority and mischaracterised two real cases in the opening brief of a defamation appeal concerning a Netflix documentary. The court assumed generative AI was responsible.

sources.label: Lichfield v. Kubler, No. 25-4135 (10th Cir. 27 Jul 2026), published opinion (Tenth Circuit)

summary: Affirming dismissal of a defamation suit over a Netflix documentary, the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit noted that the appellant's brief cited a case that does not exist and misdescribed two others. Assuming generative AI was responsible, the court issued a published admonishment but stopped short of the sanctions it imposed in Amarsingh v. Frontier Airlines.
fabricated: Opening Brief at 39 — one legal authority did not exist; the opinion did not name it
Opening Brief at 43 — one case was characterised in a manner wholly unsupported by the text; the opinion did not name it
Opening Brief at 45 — one case was characterised in a manner wholly unsupported by the text; the opinion did not name it

courtSaid.quote: In his Opening Brief, Lichfield included citation to a legal authority that does not exist, see Op. Br. at 39, and characterized two cases in manners wholly unsupported by the text of the opinions, see Op. Br. at 43, 45.

It should go without saying that a bare-minimum reasonable inquiry will ensure legal authorities cited in papers submitted to the court actually exist, and the quotations or propositions attributed to them also exist.
Although we assume the use of generative artificial intelligence led to the misrepresentations of legal authority, the brief here had significantly fewer errors than in Amarsingh.
The missteps in this case do not merit sanctions.

timeline.event: Published opinion recorded a nonexistent authority and two unsupported case characterisations.
Court noted reply conceded several citation errors but no corrected brief was filed.
Court credited a notice of errata filed after oral argument questioning.
Court affirmed dismissal and warned that the brief failed Rule 46.5.

whyItMatters: Lichfield marks the warning end of the Tenth Circuit spectrum. The panel found a Rule 46.5 failure, assumed generative AI caused the misstatements, and still declined sanctions because the brief had fewer errors than Amarsingh and counsel filed a notice of errata after argument. Unlike Scott or Barteca, there was no money sanction or disciplinary referral. The record is useful because it states the baseline duty in published form: existence, quotation, and proposition checks are part of even a bare-minimum inquiry.
practiceNote: If an appellee identifies a nonexistent authority, file a formal errata notice or corrected brief before argument, not only a reply footnote. Under Tenth Circuit Rule 46.5, the signer must confirm that each authority exists and that the quoted language or legal proposition appears in the source, regardless of the drafting tool used.

whyItMatters: The Dutch decision is the tracker’s first EU-member bar disposition, and it differs from Mata v Avianca and LeDoux because the discipline came through a dean complaint rather than a court sanction motion. The council treated AI citations as part of ordinary quality-of-service and core-value analysis: the advocate lacked tenancy expertise, copied AI-generated cases without reading them, failed to attend hearings, and left clients to face judges after withdrawing the references. Beside Dayal, it shows a regulator can respond to hallucinated authorities with a public reprimand and costs even where confidentiality concerns are not proved.
practiceNote: Before a Dutch advocate files AI-assisted research, each ECLI should be opened in an official database, read, and matched to the proposition in the pleading. If a correction withdraws citations, counsel should replace the legal support or explain the gap, then attend the hearing so the judge and client are not left with unsupported defences.

Ms. Stewart concedes that she violated Rule 11 by failing to properly review her submissions to this Court, resulting in dozens of false citations.

whyItMatters: LeDoux adds an expert-evidence branch to the usual fake-authority pattern. The sanction order also shows why later cooperation does not erase a Rule 11 problem: the court credited Stewart’s admissions and changed practices but still found bad faith because the volume of obvious errors consumed court and party resources. It is a useful comparator for Mitchell, where a claim chart rather than case law contained false intrinsic-record citations.
practiceNote: Counsel should not give experts AI-generated citation tables unless each article has been opened and matched to the report’s propositions. For any brief, keep a citation table showing the source, quoted passage and check date. If an opponent flags errors, withdraw or amend all affected filings, explain how each error arose, and stop filing new AI-assisted citations until the review is complete.

summary: Linden J in the High Court of England and Wales found that a litigant in person had fabricated or doctored documents and rejected his claim that they were AI hallucinations. The court imposed indemnity costs and a three-year civil restraint order, and referred him to the Attorney General and his barrister to the Bar Standards Board.

He then doctored an order of the court – the 29 April Order – and he subsequently gave false evidence to the court, in witness statements verified with statements of truth, seeking to explain his actions.

I am quite prepared to accept that Mr Lodhia used AI to create documents but what required to be explained is how the AI tool came to be generating documents which painted a false picture, and doctoring others, without any prompting to do so by Mr Lodhia.

I am therefore satisfied that the declaration which Mr Lodhia made in the 5 May statement of costs was false in the respects identified above and that his subsequent witness statements which have sought to support and explain it are also false. He was not liable to pay any of the sums claimed.

In the light of my findings about the conduct of Mr Lodhia, I have concluded that this matter should be referred to the Attorney General’s Office for consideration of whether to proceed against him for contempt of court and/or to refer the matter to the police.

whyItMatters: Lodhia is a rare AI-explanation case where the court rejected the asserted hallucination story after testing metadata, chronology and third-party evidence. Unlike Harber, where an unrepresented party filed fake tax cases, this record involved false evidence, an altered court order, costs documents and a barrister-supervision referral. It also extends Ayinde’s regulator-referral line: the litigant was referred to the Attorney General for possible contempt, while direct-access counsel and his company were sent to the BSB over supervision and practice controls.
practiceNote: AI cannot be used as an explanation for documents that a party files without reading. A litigant or direct-access team should retain originals, metadata and prompts, compare every exhibit to the source document before service, and never send an altered order or draft witness statement to a third party. If a non-lawyer works under chambers branding, supervision and retainer terms must be written down.

whyItMatters: Asif extends the Australian migration line from Valu and JNE24 to a self-represented applicant. The court could not refer ChatGPT, OpenAI or the applicant to a regulator, so the consequence was costs and a warning that AI-written late submissions may be refused. The judgment also records the judge’s own ChatGPT exchange, making the risk concrete: the tool admitted inventing details about a judgment by the same judge. Unlike Valu, the source did not identify a lawyer with filing duties; it focused on cost consequences and court procedure.
practiceNote: A self-represented migration applicant should file on time and use AI only for drafts checked against the tribunal reasons and AustLII authorities. Each cited paragraph must exist and support the stated proposition. If the applicant cannot explain a submission at the hearing, it is safer to withdraw or narrow it than to rely on a polished AI draft.

practiceNote: Before filing a Florida appeal, a self-represented party should verify each case in the Florida appellate archive or a legal database, then copy the exact passage into a citation log. caseName: Shahin v Industrial Relations Secretary on behalf of Multicultural NSW (No 2) [2026] NSWIRComm 11

summary: A Full Bench of the Industrial Relations Commission of New South Wales refused leave to appeal an unfair-dismissal decision, criticising the self-represented appellant's use of generative AI under Practice Note 33 after his submissions applied the wrong statute and his evidence about post-dismissal income was inconsistent. The bench drew adverse inferences but made no costs order.

Appeal ground said the Commissioner criticised AI-assisted drafting of submissions; the Full Bench found the actual criticism was AI use in evidence and failure to ensure truth

courtSaid.quote: The Appellant’s submissions appear to be a classic manifestation of the problems that arise from an over-reliance on the use of generative artificial intelligence by unrepresented litigants, and a failure to properly vet them
No criticism was levelled at the Appellant for using generative AI in “preparing submissions”.

The relevant criticisms at Decision [41], reflecting Practice Note 33, was in the use of generative AI in the preparation of evidence, and for failing to ensure “the truth and accuracy of materials relied upon in the matter”.
The failure to attend to the truth and accuracy of materials relied upon by a litigant (whether the product of AI or not) is self-evidently not a mere matter of practice and procedure.

whyItMatters: Shahin is an AI-evidence and self-represented-litigant record, not a fake-case sanctions order. That separates it from Valu, JNE24 and Asif, which turn on false authorities in migration litigation. The Full Bench accepted that Practice Note 33 permits AI for submissions, but drew a hard line at evidence and truth. The consequence was not costs or referral; it was rejection of an appeal ground and preservation of adverse credibility inferences. The record shows PN 33 working as a verification rule for litigants as well as lawyers.
practiceNote: Under NSW Practice Note 33, a self-represented party may use AI to draft submissions but must verify authorities and evidence references without relying only on AI. Do not use AI to generate, rephrase or strengthen witness evidence without leave. If AI helped prepare evidence or mitigation material, compare it against the documents produced and correct inconsistencies before the hearing.

Compared with Zhang v Chen, which led to personal costs and file review, Lee records a licence suspension and regulator costs in Ontario. The decision also anchors the lesson in Ontario Rule 4.06.1, which requires counsel to certify the authenticity of authorities in a factum.

court: Arizona Court of Appeals, Division One

In re Estate of Acciavatti; Dineen/Shibata v. Kotchka, No. 1 CA-CV 25-0606 PB — FindLaw opinion text

summary: The Arizona Court of Appeals affirmed a probate ruling and sanctioned self-represented appellant Jeffrey Kotchka, whose opening brief cited hallucinated and misrepresented authorities produced by generative AI. Holding that self-represented litigants must abide by the same rules, the court awarded appellee Kim Dineen the attorneys' fees and costs caused by the fake citations under A.R.S. §12-349 and ARCAP 25.
fabricated: Six of eight citations in the opening brief were deficient, including two cases that simply did not exist; the opinion did not reproduce the case names.
Mis-citation to wrong pages or paragraphs, misstated rules, unsupported principles and misrepresented case facts in the opening brief; the opinion did not enumerate them.

courtSaid.quote: More concerning, however, is Mr. Kotchka's failure to ensure the validity of legal citations in his opening brief that he obtained through use of generative artificial intelligence (“Gen-AI”), including his inclusion of hallucinated authorities.

Instead, it contains eight citations, six of which are deficient. The citation errors include the use of cases for principles that are not supported by the case, mis-citation to wrong pages or paragraphs, misstatement of rules enunciated in cases, and misrepresentation of case facts.

Thus, whether attorney or self-represented litigant, all who file documents with the courts remain directly and personally responsible for the content, accuracy, and quality of legal filings submitted to all courts, including this court.
Accordingly, citing a hallucinated case in a legal filing is sanctionable conduct.
